issues.subcategory: non-representative combined sample
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly frames the project as using a nationally representative sample, but the planned analytic sample combines a U.S.-matched sample with a large sports-wagering oversample. Unless analyses are weighted, stratified, or otherwise adjusted, the combined N=4,000 sample will not represent the U.S. population and associations involving gambling, substance use, religiosity, demographics, and moral disapproval may be biased.
issues.quote: This work will make use of an upcoming study (N=4,000) involving a representative sample of the U.S. population (n=2,500) and a sample of sports-wagering individuals in the U.S. (n=1,500).

issues.subcategory: no weighting or survey design plan
issues.description: The authors state that participants will be matched to population norms but do not specify whether YouGov sampling weights will be supplied or used, how the sports-wagering oversample will be incorporated, or whether standard errors will account for the sampling/matching design. This prevents evaluation of population representativeness and valid inference.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms.

issues.subcategory: sports-wagering oversample confounds focal gambling analyses
issues.description: A 1,500-person oversample selected specifically for recent sports wagering is included in a study testing moral incongruence for gambling. Sports bettors are likely to differ systematically from the general population in gambling frequency, gambling type, demographics, religiosity, risk-taking, and substance use. The analytic plan does not specify a sample-source indicator, stratified analyses, weights, or interactions by sample source, so gambling findings may be driven by the oversample rather than generalizable processes.
issues.quote: we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically.

issues.subcategory: proprietary quality control not auditable
issues.description: The study relies on YouGov's proprietary quality-control procedures and explicitly anticipates no response exclusions. Because the criteria are undisclosed, readers cannot evaluate inattentive responding, bots, duplicate participation, speeders, satisficing, or other data-quality threats. This is especially important for sensitive self-report items on pornography, gambling, and substances.
issues.quote: certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards. Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding.

issues.subcategory: unrealistic absence of missing-data plan
issues.description: The manuscript assumes there will be no unplanned missingness but does not describe forced-response settings, participant dropout, item nonresponse, missing panel covariates, 'prefer not to answer' responses, or how missingness will be handled in scale construction and regressions. This is a serious reporting and validity gap for a large online survey with sensitive items.
issues.quote: Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.subcategory: planned missingness and varying analytic denominators
issues.description: The design intentionally creates different analytic subsets for each behavior, but the manuscript does not specify how sample sizes will be reported, how listwise versus pairwise deletion will be handled, or how correlations involving measures available only to different subsets will be computed. This can lead to non-comparable estimates across behaviors and unclear denominators.
issues.quote: Therefore, for each analysis, we anticipate having slightly different subsets of the total sample.

issues.subcategory: conditioning on past-year use may induce selection bias
issues.description: The authors plan to administer moral disapproval and problem measures only to participants who engaged in each behavior. Because moral disapproval may itself affect whether people abstain, conditioning on use can induce selection/collider bias and restrict the range of moral disapproval. It also prevents estimating moral incongruence in the full population, including morally disapproving abstainers.
issues.quote: we will only administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to participants who report engaging in those behaviors.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent administration of moral disapproval items
issues.description: The measures section implies moral-disapproval items will be asked for each substance, while the data-screening section says moral disapproval will only be administered to participants who report engaging in those behaviors. This contradiction affects the analysis population and the interpretation of moral disapproval among users versus all respondents.
issues.quote: For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement “I believe that using ________ is morally wrong” on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

issues.subcategory: interaction term does not directly measure moral incongruence
issues.description: The manuscript defines moral incongruence as a statistical interaction between behavior frequency and moral disapproval. A moderation coefficient is not the same as a person's experienced discrepancy, conflict, distress, shame, or perceived violation of values. This operationalization may test whether disapproval changes the slope of frequency on symptoms, but it does not directly measure moral incongruence as a psychological construct.
issues.quote: moral incongruence (defined as the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior)

issues.subcategory: single-item moral disapproval measures
issues.description: Moral disapproval is assessed with one item per behavior. Single-item measures provide no reliability estimate, cannot distinguish personal moral conviction from perceived social norms, legal attitudes, health concerns, stigma, or disgust, and may not be psychometrically comparable across pornography, gambling, alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, prescription misuse, and illicit drugs.
issues.quote: Moral disapproval of gambling will be assessed using a single item consistent with above-described items for substances and pornography use.

issues.subcategory: moral disapproval wording not behavior-specific to own conduct
issues.description: The moral-disapproval items ask whether a behavior is morally wrong in general, not whether the respondent experiences their own behavior as inconsistent with their personal values. This weakens the link to the theorized construct of personal moral incongruence.
issues.quote: I believe that gambling is morally wrong.

issues.subcategory: legal status confounded with morality
issues.description: For prescription drug misuse and illicit drugs, the moral-disapproval items are confounded with illegality and non-medical misuse. Endorsement may reflect legal knowledge, perceived dangerousness, or social desirability rather than moral incongruence. This threatens comparisons with legal behaviors such as pornography, gambling, alcohol, and nicotine.
issues.quote: I believe that using illegal/illicit drugs is morally wrong.

issues.subcategory: outcome items contain moral/guilt content
issues.description: Several dependent-variable scales include guilt or moralized content. Because moral disapproval is a predictor, including guilt items in the outcome creates criterion contamination and can inflate associations between moral disapproval and 'addiction' symptoms, particularly for pornography and gambling.
issues.quote: You continue to use pornography even though you feel guilty about it.

issues.subcategory: problem gambling outcome includes guilt item
issues.description: The PGSI includes an item about guilt, which overlaps directly with moral disapproval and moral incongruence. This makes it difficult to interpret moral disapproval effects as reflecting gambling disorder symptoms rather than moralized distress.
issues.quote: Have you felt guilty about the way you gamble or what happens when you gamble?

issues.subcategory: self-perceived addiction conflated with symptom screens
issues.description: The hypotheses and framing focus on 'self-reported feelings of addiction,' but the dependent variables include heterogeneous symptom screens such as the BPS, PGSI, and modified ASSIST items. These instruments do not uniformly assess perceived addiction, and some are designed as risk/problem screens rather than subjective addiction identity. This mismatch threatens construct validity and cross-domain comparability.
issues.quote: self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography will be assessed using the Brief Pornography Screen

issues.subcategory: nonvalidated modified ASSIST for focal outcomes
issues.description: The authors substantially modify the ASSIST, add behaviors for which it is not validated, change response options, and then use averaged standardized items as outcome scores. These changes undermine the validity of the measure and make it unclear what construct is being assessed across substances, gambling, and pornography.
issues.quote: Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography, given the inclusion of other validated scales to assess these outcomes (see below), including them within the NIDA-ASSIST will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses.

issues.subcategory: invalid averaging of heterogeneous ASSIST items
issues.description: The planned ASSIST score averages standardized responses across items with different response scales, item meanings, and time frames, including past-3-month frequency items and lifetime/past-3-month concern/control items. This departs from validated ASSIST scoring and may produce distribution-dependent scores with unclear clinical meaning.
issues.quote: Responses to each of the above five items will be standardized, and an average will be taken for each substance of interest

issues.subcategory: ordinal predictors treated as interval-linear
issues.description: Behavior frequency is measured using coarse ordinal categories with unequal intervals and an open-ended top category, but the plan treats these as continuous linear predictors and multiplies them by moral disapproval. This assumes equal distances between 'once or twice,' 'monthly,' 'weekly,' 'daily,' and 'more than once per day,' which is unlikely and can distort main effects and interactions.
issues.quote: participants will report the frequency with which they have engaged in those behaviors over the past 12 months on a scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day)

issues.subcategory: frequency measures omit quantity/intensity
issues.description: For addictive behaviors and substances, frequency alone is often an inadequate exposure measure. Alcohol use without quantity, nicotine without dose, gambling without money wagered or duration, and pornography without duration/intensity may not correspond to addiction risk or moral incongruence. This weakens the interpretation of frequency-by-disapproval interactions.
issues.quote: we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed).

issues.subcategory: pornography frequency excludes partnered use
issues.description: Pornography frequency is operationalized as viewing pornography alone, whereas moral disapproval and problem items refer to pornography use more generally. Participants who view pornography with partners may be misclassified on the frequency predictor while still responding to broader disapproval/problem constructs.
issues.quote: Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner)

issues.subcategory: pornography frequency coding conflict
issues.description: The methods describe pornography frequency as coded 1 to 6 and define users as scores >1, but the supplemental measure codes the same scale 0 to 5. Under the supplemental coding, scores >1 would exclude people who viewed pornography once or twice, whereas under the methods coding it would include all past-year users. This ambiguity directly affects inclusion criteria and effective sample size.
issues.quote: participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day). Like the above-described process for the ASSIST, only participants who report viewing pornography at least once in the past 12 months (i.e., scores > 1 on the frequency measure) will complete the remaining items described below.

issues.subcategory: BPS scoring inconsistency
issues.description: The manuscript says the BPS uses a 0-to-2 response scale, but the supplemental table codes responses as 0, 2, and 4. This affects scale totals, comparability with validation studies, interpretation of cutoffs, and regression coefficients.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to the prompt, “In the last 6 months, have any of these situations happened to you in regards to your use of pornography?” by reporting the frequency they have experienced certain behaviors (e.g., “You have attempted to “cut back” or stop using pornography, but were unsuccessful.”) on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed.

issues.subcategory: PGSI scoring inconsistency
issues.description: The methods state that PGSI items are scored 0 to 3 and averaged, whereas the supplemental table codes response options as 0, 2, 4, and 5. The validated PGSI is normally summed using 0 to 3 scoring. The proposed coding and averaging are inconsistent and may invalidate severity interpretation.
issues.quote: This 9-item measure requires participants to respond to a series of questions (e.g., “Have you felt that you might have a problem with gambling?” and “Has gambling caused you any health problems, including stress or anxiety?”) on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged.

issues.subcategory: gambling frequency single item versus averaged behaviors
issues.description: The methods first state that gambling frequency will be assessed with a single item, but then state that an average across gambling behaviors will be used. The supplemental material appears to include only a global gambling item. The predictor is therefore not clearly defined.
issues.quote: We will assess gambling frequency using a single item.

issues.subcategory: unclear tobacco versus non-tobacco nicotine variables
issues.description: The manuscript says tobacco, e-cigarettes/vapes, and smokeless products will be subsumed under a single tobacco/nicotine question, but later lists tobacco and non-tobacco nicotine separately when describing outcome scores. This ambiguity affects the number of target behaviors, analyses, and variables.
issues.quote: smoked tobacco products, e-cigarettes/vapes, and smokeless tobacco products are all subsumed by our single question on tobacco/nicotine.

issues.subcategory: number of outcomes and moderation analyses does not add up
issues.description: The analytic plan refers to eight outcomes and ten moderation analyses corresponding to eight target behaviors, but the manuscript lists five substance categories plus pornography and gambling, with pornography and gambling repeated using validated scales. That totals nine moderation analyses unless another nicotine variable is separate. This ambiguity impairs preregistration precision.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 10 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest, with pornography and gambling repeated for both the NIDA-ASSIST measure and the validate measures of problematic use

issues.subcategory: equivalence region not tied to coefficient scaling
issues.description: The equivalence region is defined as δ=.11 based on a standardized beta, but the analysis plan only says focal variables will be centered, not standardized, and does not specify whether equivalence tests will use standardized coefficients. Raw interaction coefficients depend on the scales and variances of frequency, disapproval, and outcomes, so applying δ=.11 without a precise standardization procedure is invalid.
issues.quote: We will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression (Counsell & Cribbie, 2015), with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .11.

issues.subcategory: standardized interaction betas are not comparable across domains
issues.description: The SESOI is based on prior standardized interaction coefficients from pornography studies, but standardized coefficients for product terms are highly dependent on predictor distributions, base rates, reliability, and range restriction. Comparing β=.11 across pornography, gambling, alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, prescription misuse, and illicit drugs may not represent equivalent practical effects.
issues.quote: we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above

issues.subcategory: uniqueness inferred from significance pattern instead of direct comparison
issues.description: The central claim of uniqueness requires testing whether the interaction effect for pornography is statistically larger than corresponding effects for gambling and substances. The plan instead relies on separate significance/equivalence tests within each behavior. A significant effect in one model and nonsignificant or equivalent effects in others does not by itself establish that effects differ across domains, especially with different measures and sample sizes.
issues.quote: should we find that moral incongruence—defined as the interaction between moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior—only predicts self-reported problematic use of pornography, then this work would provide strong evidence for the validity of the PPMI as a unique model

issues.subcategory: data-dependent equivalence threshold
issues.description: If results contradict hypotheses, the authors plan exploratory analyses that redefine the equivalence region using the observed pornography effect's confidence interval. This makes the criterion for judging other effects partly data-dependent and can bias interpretation toward preserving a uniqueness claim.
issues.quote: we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.

issues.subcategory: alternative equivalence model changes estimand after low power
issues.description: For low-prevalence substances, the authors propose replacing a practical-null equivalence test with a test against the lower bound of a prior pornography effect. This no longer tests whether the substance interaction is null or practically null, only whether it is smaller than a prior pornography benchmark. Conclusions about absence of moral incongruence would therefore be unsupported.
issues.quote: rather than testing whether or not the effect of moral incongruence for these behaviors falls within the region of equivalence for our primary SESOI, we will test an alternative model where our equivalence region is defined by the lower bound of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate of moral incongruence in predicting self-reported addiction to pornography

issues.subcategory: power for detection conflated with power for equivalence
issues.description: The power analysis is framed around detecting an effect of f2=.015, but the key negative hypotheses require sufficient power for equivalence testing. Power to reject a zero-effect null is not the same as power to reject effects outside an equivalence interval. The manuscript does not provide equivalence-test power for the planned SESOI and sample sizes.
issues.quote: we conducted a power analysis to determine the sample size needed to reliably detect our smallest effect of interest (f2 = .015)

issues.subcategory: G*Power assumptions inadequate for moderation with restricted ordinal predictors
issues.description: The power analysis assumes a conventional linear regression with six predictors and one tested predictor, but the focal test is an interaction involving ordinal, skewed, range-restricted variables among behavior-specific subsets. Measurement reliability, prevalence, predictor distributions, and the oversample can strongly affect moderation power, so the reported achieved power may be optimistic.
issues.quote: For regression models with 6 predictors (age, gender, religiousness, moral disapproval, frequency, and the interaction of frequency and disapproval), our sample will be adequately powered

issues.subcategory: underspecified robustness analyses
issues.description: The plan to switch to supplemental latent-variable models when assumptions are 'substantially violated' is under-specified. No thresholds for violation, exact model specifications, item indicators, treatment of ordinal predictors, or criteria for prioritizing results are provided. This leaves substantial researcher degrees of freedom after seeing the data.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate.

issues.subcategory: mischaracterization of DWLS as solving regression assumption violations
issues.description: The manuscript states that DWLS does not rely on normally distributed or homoscedastic residuals. DWLS for ordinal latent-variable models has its own assumptions and does not automatically resolve nonlinearity, zero inflation, heteroskedasticity, or distributional problems in observed product-term moderation models. The proposed fallback may not address the stated assumption violations.
issues.quote: using diagonally weighted least squares estimation, as such an estimator does not rely on normally distributed or homoscedastic residuals

issues.subcategory: multiple primary tests without multiplicity plan
issues.description: The study proposes numerous moderation and equivalence tests across behaviors and outcomes but does not specify multiplicity correction or a hierarchical decision rule for primary hypotheses. This increases the risk of false-positive claims and ambiguous interpretation of mixed findings.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 10 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency

issues.subcategory: Holm adjustment described incorrectly
issues.description: The manuscript says bivariate correlations will be reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics. Holm procedures adjust p-values or significance thresholds, not the test statistics themselves. This is a reporting/statistical terminology error.
issues.quote: Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics using the psych package.

issues.subcategory: causal language from cross-sectional design
issues.description: Although the limitations section acknowledges the sample is cross-sectional, the manuscript repeatedly uses causal language such as 'influences,' 'contributor,' and 'affecting.' Cross-sectional associations cannot establish whether moral disapproval causes perceived addiction, whether problems increase moral disapproval, or whether both reflect third variables such as religiosity, shame-proneness, mental distress, legal attitudes, or social desirability.
issues.quote: we seek to establish whether moral incongruence (defined as the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior) influences self-perceived feelings of addiction

issues.subcategory: limited confounder adjustment
issues.description: The planned covariates are age, gender, and religiousness only. Many plausible common causes of moral disapproval and self-reported addiction symptoms are omitted, including political ideology, denomination, race/ethnicity, education, income, marital status, state legal context, mental distress, social desirability, and behavior severity/intensity. This limits interpretation even as association, and especially limits causal or uniqueness claims.
issues.quote: In each case, we intend on including religiousness, age, and gender as covariates

issues.subcategory: gender measured and modeled too crudely
issues.description: The analysis dichotomizes gender as male versus not-male. This collapses women and gender-diverse participants, may misclassify nonbinary respondents, and creates problems for gender-specific alcohol items. The manuscript does not specify how nonbinary, missing, or other gender categories will be handled.
issues.quote: gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)

issues.subcategory: alcohol binge item label contradicts prompt
issues.description: The supplemental materials specify that men are asked about more than 5 drinks, but the table row is labeled 'More than four drinks.' This creates ambiguity in the alcohol measure and may affect programming or interpretation.
issues.quote:
IF GENDER = MAN

In the past year, how often have you had more than 5 drinks on one occasion?

issues.subcategory: survey context and order effects not specified
issues.description: The focal measures are embedded in a larger sports-wagering survey, but the manuscript does not report item order, block order, randomization, survey length, or whether gambling-focused content precedes morality and addiction questions. Context effects could prime gambling, stigma, or addiction interpretations and bias responses.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited in late March of 2022 as a part of a larger study of sports wagering behaviors in the American populace funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming.

issues.subcategory: ethics, consent, incentives, and response rates missing
issues.description: The participant/procedure section lacks basic information needed to evaluate and replicate the study, including IRB/ethics approval, informed consent, compensation/incentives, recruitment invitations, response rate, completion rate, and exclusion flow.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms.

issues.subcategory: overstatement about CSBD caveat uniqueness
issues.description: The manuscript claims CSBD is the only disorder in any diagnostic manual with a moral-distress caveat. This is a broad nosological claim that is not demonstrated and may overlook other diagnostic exclusions or cultural/contextual caveats. The claim is used to motivate uniqueness, so overstatement weakens the theoretical premise.
issues.quote: At present, CSBD is the only recognized disorder in any diagnostic manual to include such a caveat

issues.subcategory: ICD caveat does not imply statistical uniqueness of interaction effect
issues.description: The ICD-11 statement that moral distress alone is insufficient for CSBD diagnosis concerns differential diagnosis and avoiding pathologizing moral distress. It does not logically require that a frequency-by-moral-disapproval interaction be unique to pornography or sexual behavior. The study's statistical test is therefore only indirectly related to the diagnostic rationale.
issues.quote: Ultimately, we aim to demonstrate that—consistent with the ICD-11 decision to include moral distress as a diagnostic consideration when applying a diagnosis of CSBD—the role moral incongruence in predicting feelings of dysregulation is unique to sexual behavior, in contrast with other addictions.

issues.subcategory: diagnostic and clinical implications overclaimed from community self-report
issues.description: The study uses a cross-sectional community panel and self-report screening measures, yet proposes implications for CSBD diagnostic validity and false-positive clinical diagnoses. Without clinical interviews, treatment-seeking samples, diagnostic adjudication, or longitudinal impairment data, the proposed evidence cannot strongly support diagnostic criteria or clinical differential diagnosis.
issues.quote: there would be additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD.

issues.subcategory: substance categories are heterogeneous and not diagnostic entities
issues.description: The manuscript treats broad categories such as 'illegal/illicit drugs' and 'prescription drugs for non-medical reasons' as comparable to recognized addictive disorders. These categories combine pharmacologically and socially distinct substances with different legal statuses, dependence liabilities, moral meanings, and symptom profiles, weakening construct validity and comparability.
issues.quote: substance use disorders (i.e., alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, illicit substances, and prescription drug misuse)

issues.subcategory: time-frame mismatch across predictors and outcomes
issues.description: Predictors and outcomes use different time frames: past-year frequency, current moral disapproval, past-3-month ASSIST problem items, last-6-month BPS items, lifetime/past-3-month ASSIST concern/control items, and past-12-month PGSI items. These mismatches complicate interpretation of associations and comparisons across behaviors.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to three frequency based questions that assess problematic use (“In the past three months, how often have you had a strong desire or urge to use or engage in the following?”, “In the past three months, how often has your use of or engagement in the following led to health, social, legal, or financial problems for you?”, and “During the past 3 months, how often have you failed to do what was normally expected of you because of your use of or engagement in the following?”)

issues.subcategory: self-report sensitivity and social desirability unaddressed
issues.description: Pornography use, illegal drug use, prescription misuse, gambling problems, and moral disapproval are sensitive topics prone to underreporting and socially desirable responding. The design contains no plan for anonymity checks, social desirability measurement, indirect questioning, validity checks, or sensitivity analyses for underreporting.
issues.quote: The primary focus of this project is to assess the prevalence of sports-wagering behaviors in the American public and how those behaviors relate to a wide variety of other behavioral addiction symptoms, substance use behaviors, and general mental well-being.

issues.subcategory: primary outcome hierarchy unclear
issues.description: Pornography and gambling each have both modified ASSIST outcomes and validated scale outcomes, but the manuscript does not clearly specify which is primary for hypothesis testing, equivalence decisions, or conclusions about uniqueness. Multiple outcome options increase analytic flexibility and can produce conflicting results.
issues.quote:
Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items
Gambling Behavior | Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items

issues.subcategory: linear regression may be inappropriate for zero-inflated bounded symptom scales
issues.description: The outcomes are bounded ordinal or summed screening scales likely to be highly skewed and zero-inflated in community samples. OLS moderation may yield inefficient or biased estimates and invalid standard errors; the proposed assumption checks and optional latent models do not provide a clear primary generalized-model alternative.
issues.quote: As a primary test of our key hypotheses, we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function in the stats package for R statistical software

issues.subcategory: model equations and coding details incomplete
issues.description: The analysis plan does not provide full regression equations, coding for categorical covariates beyond binary gender, centering/standardization details for outcomes and product terms, handling of survey weights, or how standardized coefficients and confidence intervals will be obtained. These omissions reduce reproducibility of the registered report.
issues.quote: focal predictors (behavioral frequency measures) and moderators (moral disapproval questions) will be centered and their interaction term calculated.
